subject: history_social
passage: Along the shores of the Hawaiian Islands, people built loko kuapa, fishponds enclosed by walls of stacked stone and coral on shallow reef flats. Wooden gates in the walls let small fish swim in from the sea but kept the larger, fattened fish from escaping, so the ponds could yield fish all year. Many historians link the building of such ponds to the ambitions of powerful chiefs, who controlled the ponds' harvests. Archaeologist Keoni Kamaka argues, however, that along one stretch of coast new ponds were built mainly in response to the growing number of people living nearby.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Kamaka's argument?

choices.A: The dates of new ponds along that coast closely track increases in the number of house sites near the shore.
choices.B: The fish raised in the ponds were mostly mullet and milkfish, both of which feed on algae growing in the water.
choices.C: Fishpond walls along that stretch of coast were rebuilt several times after being damaged by storms.
choices.D: Most new ponds along that coast were built within a few years after a new chief took control of the area.

explanation.why: Kamaka connects the building of new ponds to a rising local population rather than to chiefs' ambitions. Support must show that pond building rose and fell with the number of people. If the dates of new ponds track increases in nearby house sites, pond building followed population growth.
explanation.A: Correct. New ponds appeared as house sites near the shore increased, linking pond building to a growing local population.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The kinds of fish raised do not show whether population growth or chiefly power led to new ponds.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Repairs after storms say nothing about why new ponds were built in the first place.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Ponds built soon after new chiefs took power would support the usual explanation that Kamaka disputes; this weakens his argument.
